meta.title: Jane Street security interview drill
meta.note: Short answers only. Full answers live in the linked block. 'js' marks questions reported in a Jane Street loop or your own online assessment.

items.q: From a log, track consecutive failed login attempts for one user; then extend it to all users.
items.short: Stream the lines, parse into (time, user, result), keep a per-user counter that resets on success, emit when the run hits the threshold. Dict of counters for all users.
followups: Now only count failures inside a 5-minute sliding window.
What breaks at ten million lines, and what do you change?
items.wrong: Loading the whole file into a list and sorting it, then being unable to extend to a sliding window without rewriting.

items.q: Fill in `def brute_force_detect(entries): pass` where entries is a list of log-like strings.
items.short: Ask what counts as brute force (N failures per user or per source in a window), parse defensively, use a deque or window per key, return the offenders with evidence.
followups: Per source IP as well as per user?
How do you test it with an edge case?
items.wrong: Assuming a fixed line format and never asking what threshold or window the interviewer has in mind.

items.q: What does `yield` do, and why would you use a generator in a log tool?
items.short: It makes a lazy iterator that keeps state between values, so you process a file in constant memory, one line at a time.
followups: What do you lose compared with a list?
How would you compose several generator stages?
items.wrong: Describing it as 'like return but keeps going' with no mention of memory or laziness.

items.q: What is the GIL, and when do threads actually help in Python?
items.short: One thread runs Python bytecode at a time per process; threads help I/O-bound work because the GIL is released while blocking, not CPU-bound work, which needs multiprocessing.
followups: Where does asyncio fit?
Your log parser is slow. Threads, processes, or neither?
items.wrong: 'Python can't do concurrency' or recommending threads to speed up a CPU-bound regex loop.

items.q: Why is `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)` with a formatted string dangerous, and what do you do instead?
items.short: The shell parses the string, so attacker-controlled text becomes command injection; pass a list of arguments with shell=False, or shlex.quote if you must use the shell.
followups: Same question for pickle and yaml.load.
Why is comparing a token with == a bug?
items.wrong: Sanitising the string with a blocklist of characters rather than avoiding the shell.

items.q: Two users logged in from countries 5,000 km apart within ten minutes. Detect impossible travel across a log.
items.short: Sort events per user by time, compare consecutive pairs, compute distance over time and flag when implied speed exceeds a plausible threshold; handle VPNs and shared accounts as known false positives.
followups: Where do the coordinates come from, and what if the GeoIP is wrong?
Complexity?
items.wrong: Flagging any two different countries without considering the time gap or VPN egress.

items.q: Here is a shell with logs from several workstations. Something happened. Find out what, out loud.
items.short: Read a few lines of each format, establish a baseline, find the anomaly (failed logins, odd parent-child process, new service), pivot on the IP, account and time window, and narrate a theory plus what would disprove it.
followups: What is your leading theory right now?
Summarise it for the CEO in four sentences.
items.wrong: Grepping for 'error' immediately and declaring a conclusion from the first odd line.

items.q: Write the incident briefing for the CEO.
items.short: Four sentences: what happened, how they got in, what they reached, what we are doing. No event IDs, no jargon, one clear ask if there is one.
followups: What do you leave out, and why?
What if you are not yet sure of the entry point?
items.wrong: A chronological list of log events with technique names.

items.q: Which Windows event IDs tell the story of a compromise, and what does each mean?
items.short: 4625 failed logon, 4624 success (type 3 network, 10 RDP), 4688 process creation, 4698 scheduled task, 7045 new service, 4672 special privileges, 1102 audit log cleared, plus Sysmon 1/3/10 and PowerShell 4104.
followups: Which logon type would pass-the-hash show?
What does 1102 right after lateral movement tell you?
items.wrong: Knowing 4624/4625 only and nothing about process creation or persistence events.

items.q: What makes a password strong, and how would you estimate its complexity?
items.short: Entropy from how it was generated, not how it looks: length times log2 of the alphabet if random; human patterns are far smaller. Crack time is 2^entropy over the guess rate, which depends on the hash.
followups: Eight random lowercase letters against NTLM versus bcrypt?
Why does the hash matter as much as the password?
items.wrong: Reciting 'eight characters, upper, lower, digit, symbol' as the definition of strong.

items.q: You are implementing a password manager. How does it store passwords, and where does the key come from?
items.short: Vault encrypted with a key derived from the master password via a slow KDF (Argon2id or PBKDF2 with high iterations) plus salt; zero-knowledge, so the server never sees the key; secrets in memory only while unlocked.
followups: What about the second device?
How do you handle a forgotten master password?
items.wrong: Storing the master password hashed on the server and encrypting the vault with a server-side key.

items.q: How does TOTP turn a secret into a changing code, and how does it cope with clock drift?
items.short: HMAC of the shared secret over the current 30-second time step, truncated to six digits; the server accepts a window of adjacent steps to tolerate drift.
followups: Why is TOTP still phishable?
What does a hardware key do differently?
items.wrong: 'It is random' or anything that does not mention the shared secret and the time counter.

items.q: Walk through the full data flow when a user opens a website and logs in. POST or GET for the credentials, and why?
items.short: DNS, TCP, TLS handshake, HTTP request, server auth, session cookie set with Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite. POST, because GET puts credentials in URLs, history, logs and Referer headers, and is cacheable.
followups: Where in that flow does CSRF live?
What does the session cookie's SameSite attribute change?
items.wrong: 'POST is more secure because it is encrypted' (both are inside TLS; the difference is where the data lands).

items.q: Describe the TLS handshake.
items.short: ClientHello with supported suites and key share, ServerHello picks and sends its key share and certificate, both derive the session keys via (EC)DHE, server proves possession, encrypted application data; TLS 1.3 does it in one round trip with forward secrecy.
followups: What gives forward secrecy, exactly?
How does certificate pinning change the trust model?
items.wrong: 'The server sends its public key and the client encrypts a session key with it' (that is RSA key exchange, no forward secrecy, gone in 1.3).

items.q: Explain the length-extension attack and what it says about using a hash as a MAC.
items.short: Merkle-Damgård hashes expose their internal state as the output, so from H(secret||msg) you can compute H(secret||msg||pad||extra) without the secret; that is why H(key||msg) is not a MAC and HMAC exists.
followups: Which hashes are immune?
Where would you see this in a real app?
items.wrong: Confusing it with a collision attack or saying SHA-256 is 'secure so it is fine'.

items.q: XSS versus CSRF: what is the difference, and what fixes each?
items.short: XSS runs attacker script in the victim's page (fix: output encoding, CSP, HttpOnly); CSRF makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request the user did not intend (fix: SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, checking Origin).
followups: Why does HttpOnly not stop CSRF?
Does SameSite=Lax stop all CSRF?
items.wrong: Describing both as 'injecting stuff' or saying input validation fixes CSRF.

items.q: What is SSRF, and why is it worse in the cloud?
items.short: The server is tricked into making a request on the attacker's behalf, reaching internal services; in the cloud it can hit the metadata endpoint and steal instance credentials, which is why IMDSv2 requires a session token.
followups: How do you defend an app that legitimately fetches user-supplied URLs?
What did IMDSv2 actually change?
items.wrong: Treating it as 'just block 127.0.0.1' without allow-listing destinations or mentioning metadata.

items.q: A detector is 99% accurate and the real event is one in ten thousand. What fraction of its alerts are real?
items.short: Under one percent. Per million sessions: ~99 true positives and ~10,000 false positives, so precision is driven by the base rate, not the accuracy.
followups: So what do you change in the pipeline?
How does this apply to a prompt-injection classifier?
items.wrong: 'About 99%' (confusing accuracy with precision).

items.q: Why is a 128-bit hash only 64 bits strong against collisions?
items.short: The birthday bound: with N possible outputs you expect a collision after about the square root of N samples, so 2^128 gives roughly 2^64 collision resistance.
followups: What does this mean for 96-bit random GCM nonces?
For a 64-bit identifier in a busy system?
items.wrong: 'Because half the bits are used for something else' or not knowing the square-root relationship.

items.q: What happens when you type a URL and press enter, down to the packets?
items.short: DNS resolution (cache, resolver, recursion), TCP three-way handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP request and response, rendering; at each step name where ARP, routing and NAT happen.
followups: Where could an attacker on the same Wi-Fi intervene?
What does DNS over HTTPS change?
items.wrong: Stopping at 'the browser sends an HTTP request' with no transport or resolution detail.

items.q: How would you detect a port scan, a DDoS, and network-side brute force from traffic alone?
items.short: Port scan: one source, many ports or hosts, SYNs without completion, fan-out rate. DDoS: volume and source entropy against baseline. Brute force: many auth attempts to one service from one or many sources in a window.
followups: How do you separate a slow scan from noise?
What is the trade-off of blocking automatically?
items.wrong: Relying on a single-threshold alert with no baseline and no notion of rate or fan-out.

items.q: Name five Linux binaries that are two letters long.
items.short: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, dd, du, df, ps, su, sh, bc, wc, ln, od, nl, tr, vi, ar, id.
followups: Which of those would you worry about seeing in a web server's process tree?
What does dd let an attacker do?
items.wrong: Freezing, or listing three and stopping.

items.q: kill -15 versus kill -9. How do you kill a process properly?
items.short: SIGTERM asks and can be handled (cleanup); SIGKILL cannot be caught and leaves no cleanup. TERM first, then KILL. A process in D state or a zombie is not fixed by signals.
followups: Before you kill suspected malware, what do you capture?
What does SIGHUP conventionally mean?
items.wrong: 'kill -9 is just the stronger version, use that.'

items.q: How is a container isolated? Namespaces, cgroups, seccomp.
items.short: Namespaces partition what a process sees (PID, mount, net, user), cgroups limit what it uses, capabilities slice root, seccomp filters syscalls; the shared kernel is the weak point, so untrusted code gets gVisor or a microVM.
followups: How does this map to Jane Street's agent sandbox?
Why do user namespaces matter most?
items.wrong: 'A container is a lightweight VM.'

items.q: Logs suggest an unauthorised process is running. How do you confirm it and what do you look at?
items.short: ps/top for the process, /proc/<pid>/exe and cmdline and maps, its parent, open files and network sockets (lsof, ss), who started it and when, whether the binary is deleted or from a user-writable path; capture before you kill.
followups: The binary shows as (deleted). What does that tell you?
How would a rootkit hide from ps?
items.wrong: Killing it immediately and reimaging, destroying the evidence.

items.q: You are installing Windows across the company. What do you change or configure on the out-of-the-box OS?
items.short: Join to AD/Entra with a hardened baseline: remove local admin, LAPS, Credential Guard, BitLocker with TPM+PIN, application control (WDAC/AppLocker), ASR rules, EDR, disable legacy protocols (NTLMv1, SMBv1, LLMNR), PowerShell logging, host firewall, patching and Secure Boot.
followups: What would you skip for the first wave, and why?
What breaks when you turn off NTLM?
items.wrong: A list of consumer tips (antivirus, strong password) with no identity, credential-protection or application-control content.

items.q: How do you detect pass-the-hash?
items.short: 4624 logon type 3 with NTLM where Kerberos is expected, logon process NtLmSsp, admin accounts authenticating from workstations to many hosts, plus Sysmon 10 LSASS access that preceded it; prevent with Credential Guard, LAPS, tiered admin.
followups: Why does Credential Guard help?
Pass-the-hash versus pass-the-ticket?
items.wrong: 'Look for the hash in the logs' (the hash is never logged; you detect the authentication pattern).

items.q: What is Kerberoasting, and how do you detect and prevent it?
items.short: Any domain user requests service tickets for accounts with SPNs and cracks them offline; detect 4769 with RC4 encryption or bursts of ticket requests; prevent with long random service-account passwords, gMSAs, AES-only.
followups: Why does RC4 matter here?
What is the golden-ticket version of this problem?
items.wrong: Describing it as 'attacking Kerberos' with no mention of SPNs or offline cracking.

items.q: Where does Active Directory Certificate Services go wrong, and what is ESC1?
items.short: Misconfigured templates: ESC1 lets a low-privileged user request a certificate for any identity (enrollee supplies subject plus client-auth EKU), which is instant impersonation; audit templates and issuance events, remove the flag, require approval.
followups: What is ESC8?
How would you detect abuse after the fact?
items.wrong: Not knowing ADCS is an attack surface at all.

items.q: Secure Boot versus measured boot: what does each actually guarantee?
items.short: Secure Boot blocks unsigned or tampered early-boot code via a signature chain; measured boot records what ran into TPM PCRs so you can prove it later (and BitLocker can seal to it). One prevents, the other attests.
followups: Why does changing boot config prompt for the BitLocker recovery key?
What does a DMA attack bypass?
items.wrong: Using the two terms interchangeably.

items.q: IAM role versus policy, and how allow and deny are evaluated.
items.short: A policy is the permission document; a role is an identity that can be assumed and carries policies. Explicit deny wins, then any allow, default deny; SCPs and permission boundaries cap what an allow can grant.
followups: What is a confused-deputy problem in cross-account roles?
How do you find over-privileged roles at scale?
items.wrong: 'Roles are for people, policies are for services.'

items.q: How do you prevent a supply-chain attack through dependencies and CI?
items.short: Lock files and pinned versions, SCA with provenance and signatures, pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, isolated and short-lived CI credentials, SBOMs so you can answer 'are we affected' in minutes, and treat tool registries (including MCP servers) as dependencies.
followups: Walk me through Log4j day one at a firm with an SBOM versus without.
What did the 2026 LiteLLM compromise change about your answer?
items.wrong: 'Scan for vulnerabilities' with nothing about provenance, pinning or the build pipeline itself.

items.q: Design a secret-storage system for engineers and services.
items.short: Central vault with HSM-backed root, short-lived dynamic credentials over static ones, identity-based access (workload identity, not shared tokens), audit of every read, rotation on exposure, and pre-commit scanning so secrets never reach the repo.
followups: How does a service prove who it is to the vault?
What do you do the day a key is pushed to a public repo?
items.wrong: Encrypting a config file with a key stored next to it.

items.q: Scenario: a malware incident on a corporate system. Lead it.
items.short: Verify the alert, contain (isolate the host, preserve memory and disk), scope (who else has the hash, the C2, the account), eradicate, recover from known-good, then the lessons; communicate to the business in parallel.
followups: The user says they were just testing something.
Legal asks whether to notify. What do you tell them?
items.wrong: Reimaging first, which destroys the evidence and leaves you unable to scope.

items.q: An AWS access key was pushed to a public repository. First five minutes.
items.short: Rotate or disable the key immediately (do not just delete the commit), check CloudTrail for use since exposure, scope what it could reach, rotate anything it could have read, then fix the root cause with pre-commit scanning.
followups: It was used from an unknown IP four minutes after the push. Now what?
How do you prevent the next one?
items.wrong: Force-pushing the commit away and assuming the key is safe because it is no longer visible.

items.q: An internal AI agent ran a command it should not have. Respond.
items.short: Treat it as a compromised service identity: revoke its tokens and sessions, pull its action log (AI-originated calls are identifiable), find the trigger and check for indirect injection in its context, roll back changes, then tighten the allow-list and add a regression test.
followups: What is the forensic record here?
How do you stop engineers switching the control off?
items.wrong: Treating it as a model bug to be prompt-engineered away rather than an identity and permissions incident.

items.q: A strategy is sending bad orders during market hours. Respond.
items.short: Kill switch first (a prepared control), then establish what is in the market and reconcile from FIX logs, scope to the strategy or venue rather than halting everything if you safely can, loop in the desk, risk and compliance, then root-cause assuming a deploy or config change.
followups: Why is this order different from a corporate incident?
What does the Knight Capital story teach about the deploy?
items.wrong: Starting with root-cause analysis while orders are still going out.

items.q: Threat-model this system, live.
items.short: Shostack's four questions out loud: what are we building (assets, flows, trust boundaries), what can go wrong (STRIDE per element, attack paths to the crown jewels), what are we doing about it, did we do a good job. Leave three concrete actions.
followups: What would you skip, and why?
How do you make this stick with the team?
items.wrong: Listing generic threats (DDoS, phishing) that do not come from the data flow in front of you.

items.q: Design a firm-wide permissioning system.
items.short: Decide subjects (people, services, agent identities), resources and conditions; pick ReBAC with ABAC conditions for a desk-structured firm; deny by default, JIT elevation, separation of duties, information barriers as non-overridable negative checks; one decision point, full decision log, data-driven access reviews.
followups: How do you model an information barrier between two desks?
What do you not model on day one?
items.wrong: 'RBAC with an admin role' and nothing about agents, barriers or audit.

items.q: Design a vulnerability-management programme.
items.short: Inventory and SBOM first, scan with dedupe and validation, prioritise by exploitability (KEV, EPSS, reachability, asset criticality) not CVSS, SLAs by tier with compensating controls for the trading path, automate triage and ticketing, measure crown-jewel exposure trending down.
followups: A critical CVSS on an isolated test host versus a medium on the exchange gateway?
What does automation never do here?
items.wrong: 'Patch everything critical within 7 days' with no inventory, prioritisation or change-window reality.

items.q: Design the security automation for a SOC. What first, what never?
items.short: Enrich always, triage and score mostly, contain only with high confidence and reversibility and a never-auto list, remediate last with human approval for the irreversible; idempotent, logged under its own identity, dry-run mode, playbooks in version control with tests.
followups: What goes on the never-auto list at a trading firm?
How do you measure it?
items.wrong: Starting with auto-isolation of hosts before the enrichment and triage layers exist.

items.q: A team has never threat-modelled. How do you start, and how do you make it a habit?
items.short: Run it on their own system in 45 minutes with the four questions, let the system owner lead, leave three actions, and make the next session lighter so it becomes routine rather than a gate.
followups: A senior engineer says it is paperwork. What do you say?
How does your tooling fit in without replacing the conversation?
items.wrong: Proposing a framework rollout, training programme and template library.

items.q: "I don't want 2FA. My passwords are unique and I'm good at spotting phishing." Respond.
items.short: Acknowledge the real point (unique passwords beat most people), then the gap: a breach of the service, a session token theft, or one convincing phish defeats any password; choose the lowest-friction phishing-resistant option for them and offer to set it up.
followups: They are a senior trader and still say no.
Which second factor would you pick for them, and why?
items.wrong: Lecturing about policy or citing a compliance requirement.

items.q: Describe your own personal security setup, and how you help others improve theirs.
items.short: Specific and proportionate: password manager, hardware keys on the accounts that matter, auto-updates, full-disk encryption, DMARC on your own domain; for others, start from what they value and remove friction rather than adding rules.
followups: What do you deliberately not do, and why?
Is a password notebook ever acceptable?
items.wrong: A maximalist list that implies everyone should lock down everything.

items.q: You are the new CISO of a small firm. First priorities?
items.short: Know the crown jewels and who can reach them, get identity right (MFA, admin tiering, offboarding), get visibility (logging on the things that matter), patch the exposed edge, and have a rehearsed incident plan; then measure and iterate.
followups: What do you deliberately defer?
How do you know it is working in six months?
items.wrong: Buying a SIEM and writing policies before knowing what the firm actually has.

items.q: Tell me about yourself, in two minutes.
items.short: Lead with what you build: product security for a trading platform, the remediation bot and sandboxed verifier, teaching 450 engineers; one line on the path; why this role, specifically. Title last or not at all.
followups: Why leave an SVP role?
What do you want to be doing in two years?
items.wrong: Opening with the title and a chronological CV walk.

items.q: Why Jane Street?
items.short: Something specific and true: a programmers-first security team, a firm that builds in-house and will let you build, the agent programme you can contribute to as a peer, the measured culture; not prestige or compensation.
followups: Why a trading firm over an AI lab or big tech?
What worries you about joining?
items.wrong: 'It's a top firm with brilliant people.'

items.q: Tell me about a time you were wrong.
items.short: A real technical or judgement mistake, what the consequence was, what you changed in how you work, told without deflection or excessive self-flagellation.
followups: How did you tell the people affected?
What would you do differently today?
items.wrong: A humble-brag ('I worked too hard') or blaming the context.

items.q: What would you do in your first 90 days?
items.short: Listen and map (on-call, existing detections, crown jewels versus what is monitored), ship one small useful thing with the team by day 60, then propose with evidence by day 90; say what you would not do (arrive with a programme).
followups: What is the small thing, concretely?
How do you avoid stepping on the team?
items.wrong: A strategy, an operating model, and a reorg.

items.q: What questions do you have for us?
items.short: Specific, homework-showing questions: how the sandbox allow-list has evolved, how detections get from idea to production here, what the team wishes it had automated last year, how a security engineer's first project usually gets chosen.
items.wrong: 'What is the culture like?' or nothing.

items.q: A suspicious hash appears in a log. What is your first step, and then?
items.short: Reputation and fleet search first (no detonation), then static (strings, imports, signatures) in an isolated VM, then sandbox detonation for behaviour, then scope and respond with the indicators and the technique.
followups: Static versus dynamic: what does each miss?
The sample sleeps for ten minutes in the sandbox. Why?
items.wrong: Running it on your own machine to see what it does.

items.q: You have a memory image from a possibly compromised machine. How do you analyse it?
items.short: Volatility: process list and scan for hidden processes, parent-child tree, network connections, injected code via malfind, unlinked DLLs, command lines and handles; look for processes with deleted backing files or RWX private pages.
followups: Why memory before disk?
What lives only in memory?
items.wrong: Running antivirus against the image file.

items.q: A support agent reads tickets and can issue refunds up to $500. Where does it go wrong, and where do you stop it?
items.short: The ticket is untrusted content; an indirect injection asks for a refund. Make eligibility and the cap deterministic code the model calls, scope the authority (a capability, not a payment token), human approval for the irreversible; the filter is a layer, not the control.
followups: Name the three legs of the lethal trifecta here and which you cut.
What happens to the model's output after it is done?
items.wrong: Leading with a prompt-injection filter and 'never reveal your instructions' in the system prompt.

items.q: Direct versus indirect prompt injection. Why is a secret system prompt not a control?
items.short: Direct is the user; indirect is an instruction hidden in content the model reads later. Prompts leak, and even a secret one does not stop the agent taking the harmful action, so authorisation and secrets stay out of the prompt entirely.
followups: Describe the dual-LLM pattern.
Which OWASP risk is this, by name?
items.wrong: Treating prompt hardening as the primary defence.

items.q: How do you contain an agent at the OS level, and how does Jane Street do it?
items.short: Namespaces and a mount sandbox, isolated network stack, seccomp, dropped capabilities; Jane Street moved from a deny-list to an allow-list (bwrap for files, pasta for network, seccomp-learned profile), with an LLM classifier for anything outside the list and per-employee AI identities for attribution.
followups: Their engineers switched the sandbox off when it blocked them. What do you change?
Why does identifiable RPC matter?
items.wrong: 'Run it in Docker.'

items.q: An MCP tool's description contains instructions aimed at the model. How does it reach the model, and what stops it?
items.short: Tool definitions enter the context before any call, so a malicious description is an injection that lands first; pin and diff tool definitions, show the full text to the approver, scope credentials per tool, run servers unprivileged, OAuth 2.1 with audience validation for remote ones.
followups: What is a rug pull here?
How do you keep a second client from using a stored token?
items.wrong: Assuming tool descriptions are metadata the model never sees as instructions.

items.q: Your prompt-injection classifier catches 95% in eval. Do you ship it?
items.short: As one layer, yes; as the control, no. The 5% is the design problem, and with a low base rate most of its alerts will be false, so spend the effort on least privilege and human gates for the actions that matter.
followups: Walk me through the base-rate arithmetic.
What would make you trust the 95% number?
items.wrong: 'Yes, 95% is good' or 'No, it must be 100%.'

items.q: Why can't you put an inline inspection device on the order path, and what do you do instead?
items.short: The inspection is the latency, and microseconds are the product; isolate the path physically, validate at the gateway endpoints, monitor from taps and mirror ports, and keep the risk checks deterministic and fast.
followups: Where do pre-trade risk checks live, then?
How does this change your detection design?
items.wrong: Proposing a TLS-terminating proxy or IPS on the hot path.

items.q: How would you connect a new strategy to an exchange, securely?
items.short: Private cross-connect or co-lo, certified sessions with vault-held venue credentials, pre-trade risk and a kill switch on the path (15c3-5 style), the trading network segmented from corporate and research, A/B feed arbitration, tap-based monitoring with time-synced tamper-evident order logs, failover that never double-sends.
followups: What did Knight Capital get wrong, specifically?
What is a crossed book and why would you care?
items.wrong: A generic 'secure network design' with no risk checks, kill switch or latency awareness.

items.q: What should a security engineer know about FIX?
items.short: Tag=value session protocol over TCP with logon, heartbeats and sequence numbers; weak native auth so it runs over private links or TLS; FIX logs are the forensic record of what was ordered and when, so their integrity and timestamps matter.
followups: What attack does sequence-number handling defend against?
Why does PTP matter to you as a security engineer?
items.wrong: 'It's an encrypted protocol for trading' (it is not natively encrypted).

items.q: We write a lot in OCaml. How do you feel about that?
items.short: Why they use it (types catch bugs at compile time, GC gives memory safety, OxCaml modes buy performance back), that you have read the ecosystem and written a little, and that their own pages say most engineers learn it after joining.
followups: Read this snippet aloud and tell me what it does.
Why is verifying AI-written OCaml easier than AI-written Python?
items.wrong: Faking fluency, or dismissing it as irrelevant to security.

items.q: Take 'we should detect Kerberoasting' to a rule in production.
items.short: Hypothesis and the evidence it leaves (4769, RC4, bursts), confirm you have the log and fields fleet-wide, write it narrowly on the attacker's invariant, test with a true positive and a week of production noise, tune with documented exclusions, ship with a runbook, measure and retire.
followups: Which ElastAlert rule type is this?
Your rule fires 200 times a day with one true positive. Now what?
items.wrong: Writing the query and shipping it with no test data, runbook or precision measurement.

items.q: Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC and what each actually stops.
items.short: SPF: DNS list of allowed senders, checked against the envelope sender, breaks on forwarding. DKIM: signature over headers and body with the key in DNS. DMARC: requires the visible From to align with a passing SPF or DKIM domain and publishes a policy; only DMARC at reject stops display-domain spoofing.
followups: Why do most domains sit at p=none?
How does BEC get past all three?
items.wrong: 'SPF stops spoofing' (it checks the envelope, not the From the user sees).

items.q: One host is beaconing to an unknown domain. How do you confirm it and what do you look at?
items.short: Group connections by source and destination, look at the inter-arrival distribution (tight period plus small jitter), consistent small payloads, a young or low-reputation domain nobody else talks to, JA3/JA4 matches; then the process behind the socket on the host.
followups: Attackers add jitter. What survives?
How is DNS tunnelling different?
items.wrong: Blocking the domain and closing the ticket without finding the process or scoping other hosts.

items.q: What is the pyramid of pain, and how does it decide what you build?
items.short: Indicators ranked by attacker cost to change: hashes, IPs, domains at the bottom; artefacts and tools in the middle; TTPs on top. Build behavioural detections first and measure coverage against ATT&CK, use indicators for fast wins with an expiry.
followups: Give a behavioural detection for the phishing chain.
How do you report coverage to leadership?
items.wrong: Measuring the programme by number of rules or number of IOCs ingested.

items.q: A system owner says the risk you found is not real. What do you do?
items.short: Ask them to walk you through why, because they may know a control you missed; if the risk stands, demonstrate it concretely rather than assert it, offer the smallest fix that works, and document the decision either way with the rationale.
followups: They still say no and they outrank you.
How do you keep the relationship?
items.wrong: Escalating to management or citing policy as the first move.

items.q: How would you scale threat modelling across hundreds of internal systems with a small team?
items.short: Start with the arithmetic, then: deterministic extraction of the data-flow model from typed sources, a language model for enumeration grounded in the firm's own threat library, deterministic ranking against the asset list, a human decision with rationale per item, and an evaluation harness built before the tool.
followups: What goes wrong with AI-generated threat models?
How do you know the output is any good?
items.wrong: 'Use an LLM to generate threat models from the design docs.'

items.q: What is wrong with AI-generated threat models?
items.short: Plausible hallucinated threats, generic floods with low precision, missing context the model cannot infer, blindness to business-logic threats, the input documents as an injection surface, confidentiality of the architecture, no ground truth to evaluate against, staleness, diluted ownership, non-determinism, and the adoption failure when it adds friction.
followups: Pick the two worst and tell me the fix.
Why does the sandbox story from their podcast apply here?
items.wrong: Enthusiasm without a failure list.
